citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The facility did not perform complete daily observation of all animals to assess their health and well-being. An adult New
Guinea singing dog had a skin lesion on the inside aspect of the left hind leg (medial stifle). The lesion appeared to be
more than 24 hours old.
The facility had not identified this condition prior to the inspection. This has prevented the attending veterinarian from the
opportunity to provide timely medical care for the animal.
The facility notified the attending veterinarian during the inspection.
Daily observations of all animals to assess their health and well-being must be throughly performed from this date
forward, September 14, 2026

Multiple enclosures are not in good repair with excavated and elevated dig guards, and exposed fasteners sticking out of
surfaces.
In the enclosure housing eleven red foxes, the enclosure housing one African crested porcupine, the enclosure housing
two New Guinea singing dogs behind the house, and the enclosure housing two grey wolves, the animals have excavated
under the wire dig guard.
In the enclosures housing one kinkajou and the enclosure housing two hybrid brown bears and one tiger, there are there
are sharp metal protrusions that can injure the animals. In the kinkajou enclosure, the housing box became detached from
the backer board. This caused two screws to have the pointed end projecting into the enclosure. In the bear and tiger
enclosure there is a damaged chain-link fence dig guard that is damaged and has wire ends sticking up out of the ground.
Enclosures that are not kept in good repair can result in injury to the animals from entrapment or sharp points. Gaps
beneath the wire dig guards can allow an animal’s limb to pass through and potentially become entrapped or broken. The
sharp points can cause punctures or lacerations to the animal’s eyes, feet or skin.
The enclosures must be constructed of such material and of such strength as appropriate for the animals involved. The
housing facilities shall be maintained in good repair to protect the animals from injury and to contain the animals.

The facility does not have an effective pest control program in place to control insects and vermin. Numerous flies and
rodent droppings were observed by USDA inspectors in the food prep area on the floor and tables.
Pests can pose a hazard to the health and wellbeing of the animals by either irritating or injuring them and exposing them
to potential diseases or illness. A safe and effective program for the control of insects, ectoparasites, and avian and
mammalian pests shall be established and maintained.

In the outdoor enclosure housing two blue-and-gold macaws and one hybrid macaw, metal screws were observed
protruding from the perches where the birds had removed the surrounding wood. These sharp points are accessible to the
birds and could cause injury.
Primary enclosures must be constructed and maintained so that they have no sharp points or edges that may injure the
birds. The primary enclosures must be kept in good repair.
Correct by September 28, 2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with a facility representative.
You may appeal all or part of any inspection report by submitting a written statement contesting the findings—along with
any supporting documentation—to the Deputy Administrator. Appeals of routine, focused, or attempted inspections must
be received within 21 days of report issuance as shown by the signature line of this report.
Appeals may be sent by email to AnimalCare@usda.gov.
Appeals sent by mail should be addressed to:
Deputy Administrator
APHIS Animal Care (AC)
U.S. Department of Agriculture
2150 Centre Avenue, Building B
Mailstop #3W11
Fort Collins, CO 80526-8117
Additional Inspectors:
E RODRIGUEZ, VETERINARY MEDICAL OFFICER n
